items.stem: What is the most appropriate approach to a Paper 1 "compare and contrast" question?
items.answer: Identify both similarities and differences, linking the sources point by point
items.markingKey: Identify both similarities and differences, linking the sources point by point. Markschemes cap answers that address only similarities or only differences.

items.stem: "In a compare and contrast question, writing one paragraph on each source is the best approach." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Separate descriptions rarely compare; a running comparison linking sources point by point on similarities and differences scores more highly.
items.markingKey: Separate descriptions rarely compare; a running comparison linking sources point by point on similarities and differences scores more highly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the origin and purpose of a source affect its usefulness.
items.answer: Who produced a source and why shapes what it includes or omits; e.g. a government press release may present policy positively, so it is useful for understanding the government's position but less reliable as neutral evidence.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Who produced a source and why shapes what it includes or omits; e.g. a government press release may present policy positively, so it is useful for understanding the government's position but less reliable as neutral evidence. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Satellite images show the village was burned on 14 March. Survivors interviewed in the camp named the unit responsible."
— Report by a human rights investigation NGO (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain what makes this evidence more convincing than an unsupported claim.
items.answer: It combines independent forms of evidence – satellite imagery and multiple witness testimonies – that corroborate each other with specific details (date, unit), increasing reliability, though the NGO's purpose and access should still be considered.
items.markingKey: It combines independent forms of evidence – satellite imagery and multiple witness testimonies – that corroborate each other with specific details (date, unit), increasing reliability, though the NGO's purpose and access should still be considered. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using UN Security Council debates on Ukraine as an example, explain evaluating sources from opposing actors.
items.answer: Statements by Russia and Ukraine at the Council present opposing accounts of the war, its causes and responsibility. comparing such statements shows how origin and purpose shape claims, and own knowledge is needed to assess them
items.markingKey: Context (Statements by Russia and Ukraine at the Council present opposing accounts of the war, its causes and responsibility.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: comparing such statements shows how origin and purpose shape claims, and own knowledge is needed to assess them – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating sources from opposing actors.

items.stem: A Paper 1 source is a press release from an oil company praising its community programmes in the Niger Delta. Evaluate its usefulness for a question on the impact of MNCs on development.
items.answer: Useful: shows the company's perspective and claimed benefits (schools, clinics). Limitations: purpose is reputational, likely omits pollution and conflict; needs corroboration from NGO reports (e.g. UNEP 2011) or own knowledge. Balanced judgement.
items.markingKey: Useful: shows the company's perspective and claimed benefits (schools, clinics). Limitations: purpose is reputational, likely omits pollution and conflict; needs corroboration from NGO reports (e.g. UNEP 2011) or own knowledge. Balanced judgement.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that own knowledge is more important than the sources in answering Paper 1 evaluation questions.
items.answer: Neither is sufficient alone; the strongest answers integrate sources and own knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: provides context and counter-examples; needed for top markbands. Arguments against: questions are designed around sources; answers must engage with all relevant sources; markbands require both. Supported judgement: Neither is sufficient alone; the strongest answers integrate sources and own knowledge.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our government has built 10,000 schools in five years, the largest education expansion in the nation's history."
— Press release, Ministry of Education (adapted)

Evaluate the usefulness of the source for a study of whether a government has met the right to education.
items.answer: Useful for the government's claim and scale of investment; limitations – purpose is promotional, gives quantity not quality, says nothing about access, teachers or enrolment of girls; needs corroboration (UNESCO data, NGO reports).
items.markingKey: Useful for the government's claim and scale of investment; limitations – purpose is promotional, gives quantity not quality, says nothing about access, teachers or enrolment of girls; needs corroboration (UNESCO data, NGO reports). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "claim".
items.answer: A statement presented as true in a source, which may be supported or unsupported by evidence
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a statement presented as true in a source, which may be supported or unsupported by evidence. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is important to use own knowledge in a Paper 1 evaluation question.
items.answer: Sources give limited perspectives; own knowledge provides context, corroboration and counter-examples, allowing a balanced evaluation – answers relying only on the sources cannot reach the top markband.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sources give limited perspectives; own knowledge provides context, corroboration and counter-examples, allowing a balanced evaluation – answers relying only on the sources cannot reach the top markband. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between reliability of a source and usefulness of a source.
items.answer: Reliability is how trustworthy or accurate a source is; usefulness depends on the question – even an unreliable, biased source can be very useful for showing a particular perspective.
items.markingKey: Reliability is how trustworthy or accurate a source is; usefulness depends on the question – even an unreliable, biased source can be very useful for showing a particular perspective. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify three things you should examine when evaluating a source in Paper 1.
items.answer: Origin (author, date, place), purpose (inform, persuade), content (claims and evidence), perspective/bias, values and limitations, corroboration with other sources. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Origin (author, date, place), purpose (inform, persuade), content (claims and evidence), perspective/bias, values and limitations, corroboration with other sources. 1 mark each.

items.stem: "The origin of a source is the most important factor in judging its usefulness." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Origin is a key starting point, but usefulness must be judged against the question, content and corroboration.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: origin reveals interests and bias; official sources show positions. Arguments against: usefulness depends on the question; content and corroboration matter; biased sources reveal perspectives. Supported judgement: Origin is a key starting point, but usefulness must be judged against the question, content and corroboration. Markbands: Markbands (scaled to the marks available, five bands): top band – sharply focused, accurate knowledge of concepts, theories and specific examples, well-developed counter-claims and a clear, well-supported judgement; upper-middle – focused, relevant examples, counter-claims addressed, reasoned conclusion; middle – mostly focused, some examples and counter-claims, conclusion stated; lower – limited, mainly descriptive knowledge with little evaluation; bottom – minimal relevant knowledge, no evaluation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An argument that challenges the main thesis, which should be evaluated rather than ignored"?
items.answer: counter-claim
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of counter-claim.

items.stem: Briefly explain why using a range of examples from different regions strengthens an essay.
items.answer: It shows the argument holds across contexts, demonstrates breadth of knowledge, and avoids generalising from one case; contrasting examples can also reveal conditions under which a claim is true.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows the argument holds across contexts, demonstrates breadth of knowledge, and avoids generalising from one case; contrasting examples can also reveal conditions under which a claim is true. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between analysis and description.
items.answer: Description recounts what happened; analysis explains why it happened, its significance and how it relates to the question and concepts.
items.markingKey: Description recounts what happened; analysis explains why it happened, its significance and how it relates to the question and concepts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify three features that distinguish a top-band Paper 2 essay from a middle-band essay.
items.answer: Sustained focus on the question; detailed, accurate specific examples; well-developed counter-claims; integration of concepts/theories; clear, consistent, supported conclusion. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Sustained focus on the question; detailed, accurate specific examples; well-developed counter-claims; integration of concepts/theories; clear, consistent, supported conclusion. 1 mark each.

items.stem: A student claims that the more examples an essay lists, the higher its mark. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Markbands reward relevant, well-analysed examples; listing many examples without explanation is descriptive and scores lower.
items.markingKey: Markbands reward relevant, well-analysed examples; listing many examples without explanation is descriptive and scores lower. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using a model essay on development pathways as an example, explain the use of data as evidence.
items.answer: A strong essay compares South Korea, Chile and Ghana, using HDI and Gini data to assess outcomes of state-led versus market-led strategies. quantitative indicators support analytical claims and allow comparisons
items.markingKey: Context (A strong essay compares South Korea, Chile and Ghana, using HDI and Gini data to assess outcomes of state-led versus market-led strategies.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: quantitative indicators support analytical claims and allow comparisons – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of data as evidence.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that balance is more important than a clear argument in Paper 2 essays.
items.answer: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: counter-claims required; avoids one-sidedness. Arguments against: top band requires a consistent judgement; balance without conclusion is weak. Supported judgement: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.

items.stem: "Balance is more important than a clear argument in Paper 2 essays." Discuss.
items.answer: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: counter-claims required; avoids one-sidedness. Arguments against: top band requires a consistent judgement; balance without conclusion is weak. Supported judgement: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion. Markbands: Markbands (scaled to the marks available, five bands): top band – sharply focused, accurate knowledge of concepts, theories and specific examples, well-developed counter-claims and a clear, well-supported judgement; upper-middle – focused, relevant examples, counter-claims addressed, reasoned conclusion; middle – mostly focused, some examples and counter-claims, conclusion stated; lower – limited, mainly descriptive knowledge with little evaluation; bottom – minimal relevant knowledge, no evaluation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why counter-claims are essential in a Paper 2 essay.
items.answer: Evaluation requires considering alternative views; addressing counter-claims shows balance and allows the candidate to justify why the thesis is stronger, which is required for the higher markbands.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Evaluation requires considering alternative views; addressing counter-claims shows balance and allows the candidate to justify why the thesis is stronger, which is required for the higher markbands. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The more examples an essay lists, the higher its mark." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Markbands reward relevant, well-analysed examples; listing many examples without explanation is descriptive and scores lower.
items.markingKey: Markbands reward relevant, well-analysed examples; listing many examples without explanation is descriptive and scores lower. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a model essay on development pathways shows the use of data as evidence.
items.answer: A strong essay compares South Korea, Chile and Ghana, using HDI and Gini data to assess outcomes of state-led versus market-led strategies. quantitative indicators support analytical claims and allow comparisons
items.markingKey: Context (A strong essay compares South Korea, Chile and Ghana, using HDI and Gini data to assess outcomes of state-led versus market-led strategies.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: quantitative indicators support analytical claims and allow comparisons – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of data as evidence.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Every paragraph should answer the question, not just the topic."
— Advice from an IB teacher's guide (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, why focus on the question matters in essay writing.
items.answer: Paragraphs that discuss the topic generally without linking to the specific question (e.g. "to what extent") lose focus; each point should explicitly advance the argument.
items.markingKey: Paragraphs that discuss the topic generally without linking to the specific question (e.g. "to what extent") lose focus; each point should explicitly advance the argument. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "False or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive; disinformation is false information spread deliberately"?
items.answer: misinformation
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of misinformation.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "A case study is only useful if it happened in the last month." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Contemporary means relevant to current politics – cases from recent years are valuable, and some older cases (e.g. Rwanda 1994) remain essential context.
items.markingKey: Contemporary means relevant to current politics – cases from recent years are valuable, and some older cases (e.g. Rwanda 1994) remain essential context. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why linking each case study to several key concepts makes it more useful.
items.answer: A single case (e.g. the Belt and Road Initiative) can illustrate power, sovereignty, development and interdependence, so it can be used flexibly in different essays. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single case (e.g. the Belt and Road Initiative) can illustrate power, sovereignty, development and interdependence, so it can be used flexibly in different essays. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe the UN SDG Report and national data and explain what it reveals about using reliable data for case studies.
items.answer: The annual UN Sustainable Development Goals Report compiles data on progress towards each goal, although data gaps exist for many countries. official data provide evidence for essays, but students should recognise gaps and limitations
items.markingKey: Context (The annual UN Sustainable Development Goals Report compiles data on progress towards each goal, although data gaps exist for many countries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: official data provide evidence for essays, but students should recognise gaps and limitations – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using reliable data for case studies.

items.stem: Using Bellingcat's investigation of MH17 as an example, explain verifying information in the digital age.
items.answer: Open-source researchers used social media photos, videos and satellite images to trace the Buk missile launcher that downed flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in 2014 to a Russian military unit. it shows how publicly available information can be verified and corroborated to establish facts
items.markingKey: Context (Open-source researchers used social media photos, videos and satellite images to trace the Buk missile launcher that downed flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in 2014 to a Russian military unit.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows how publicly available information can be verified and corroborated to establish facts – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to verifying information in the digital age.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that building a case study portfolio is the most important preparation for Global Politics exams.
items.answer: A portfolio is vital, but it must be combined with conceptual understanding and practice in argument.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: essays reward specific examples; Paper 1 own knowledge; flexible use across questions. Arguments against: understanding concepts and theories equally important; essay skills and practice needed. Supported judgement: A portfolio is vital, but it must be combined with conceptual understanding and practice in argument.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "media literacy".
items.answer: The ability to access, analyse and evaluate media messages, including identifying bias and misinformation
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the ability to access, analyse and evaluate media messages, including identifying bias and misinformation. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a primary source and a secondary source.
items.answer: A primary source is original evidence from the time or actor (a treaty, speech, dataset); a secondary source interprets or analyses primary evidence (a news analysis, textbook).
items.markingKey: A primary source is original evidence from the time or actor (a treaty, speech, dataset); a secondary source interprets or analyses primary evidence (a news analysis, textbook). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Create a portfolio entry for one contemporary case study: give the case, date, actors, two linked key concepts and one theory it could support or challenge.
items.answer: E.g. Sudan civil war (2023–): SAF and RSF, UAE and other external actors, UN agencies; concepts – conflict, legitimacy, sovereignty; theory – realism (power struggle) or feminist (sexual violence). Credit accuracy and relevance.
items.markingKey: E.g. Sudan civil war (2023–): SAF and RSF, UAE and other external actors, UN agencies; concepts – conflict, legitimacy, sovereignty; theory – realism (power struggle) or feminist (sexual violence). Credit accuracy and relevance.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A good Global Politics student reads the news like a detective: Who is speaking? Who benefits? What is missing?"
— Advice in a Global Politics teacher's guide (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain how students should evaluate news sources.
items.answer: They should examine origin (who is speaking), purpose and interests (who benefits) and omissions (what is missing), checking claims against other sources.
items.markingKey: They should examine origin (who is speaking), purpose and interests (who benefits) and omissions (what is missing), checking claims against other sources. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "running comparison"?
options: A first-hand account or original document, such as a treaty text, speech or official statement
Relevant information, concepts and examples that a candidate brings from study beyond the sources provided
An argument that challenges the main thesis, which should be evaluated rather than ignored
A comparison in which similarities and differences between sources are discussed point by point, rather than describing each source separately
items.answer: A comparison in which similarities and differences between sources are discussed point by point, rather than describing each source separately
items.markingKey: D. "running comparison" is a comparison in which similarities and differences between sources are discussed point by point, rather than describing each source separately.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "One of the central ideas of the Global Politics course, such as power, sovereignty, legitimacy or interdependence, used to frame analysis"?
items.answer: key concept
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of key concept.

items.stem: What is a primary source for studying the Paris Agreement?
items.answer: The text of the Paris Agreement published by the UNFCCC
items.markingKey: The text of the Paris Agreement published by the UNFCCC. Primary sources are original documents.

One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why defining key concepts early in an essay is useful.
items.answer: Concepts such as sovereignty or legitimacy are contested; defining them clarifies the criteria for judgement and keeps the argument focused on the question.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Concepts such as sovereignty or legitimacy are contested; defining them clarifies the criteria for judgement and keeps the argument focused on the question. items.stem: Hana writes: "A biased source is useless for answering a Paper 1 question." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Biased sources can be very useful for revealing an actor's perspective, interests or rhetoric; their limitations must be acknowledged and checked against other evidence.
items.markingKey: Biased sources can be very useful for revealing an actor's perspective, interests or rhetoric; their limitations must be acknowledged and checked against other evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a topic sentence and a thesis.
items.answer: A thesis is the overall argument of the essay; a topic sentence introduces the specific point of a single paragraph, which should support or test the thesis.
items.markingKey: A thesis is the overall argument of the essay; a topic sentence introduces the specific point of a single paragraph, which should support or test the thesis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that social media posts are always unreliable and should never be used. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Social media can provide valuable first-hand evidence (e.g. videos verified by open-source investigators), but posts must be verified and corroborated.
items.markingKey: Social media can provide valuable first-hand evidence (e.g. videos verified by open-source investigators), but posts must be verified and corroborated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Read the source below.

"In the first hours after the explosion, three different videos claimed to show the scene. Two were from other countries and years earlier."
— Fact-checking organization report (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, why verification is important when building case studies.
items.answer: Misleading or recycled content spreads quickly in crises; verification (reverse image search, corroboration) prevents students from using false evidence.

items.stem: Using a model essay on whether the UN Security Council is legitimate as an example, explain the use of concepts and case studies in argument.
items.answer: A strong essay defines legitimacy (Weber, Beetham), uses the Ukraine and Gaza vetoes and peacekeeping authorisations as evidence, and evaluates reform proposals (G4, veto initiative). concepts provide criteria, while specific cases test the claim, enabling a supported judgement
items.markingKey: Context (A strong essay defines legitimacy (Weber, Beetham), uses the Ukraine and Gaza vetoes and peacekeeping authorisations as evidence, and evaluates reform proposals (G4, veto initiative).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Briefly describe disinformation during the 2016 US election and explain what it reveals about the importance of media literacy.
items.answer: US investigations found that the Russian Internet Research Agency used social media accounts to spread divisive content. state-sponsored disinformation shows why students must evaluate the origin and purpose of online information
items.markingKey: Context (US investigations found that the Russian Internet Research Agency used social media accounts to spread divisive content.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: state-sponsored disinformation shows why students must evaluate the origin and purpose of online information – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of media literacy.

items.stem: Outline one way in which NGO and government reports on Xinjiang shows corroboration of contested claims.
items.answer: Human rights NGOs describe mass detention and forced labour, while Chinese government white papers describe vocational training and counter-terrorism. candidates must weigh evidence, origin and corroboration (e.g. the 2022 OHCHR assessment) rather than accept either account at face value
items.markingKey: Context (Human rights NGOs describe mass detention and forced labour, while Chinese government white papers describe vocational training and counter-terrorism.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The best essays did not tell me everything the candidate knew about the UN. They told me what the candidate thought, and why."
— Comment attributed to a Global Politics examiner (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain what examiners look for in Paper 2 essays.
items.answer: Examiners reward argument and evaluation over knowledge dumping: a clear thesis, analysis linked to the question and justified judgement.
items.markingKey: Examiners reward argument and evaluation over knowledge dumping: a clear thesis, analysis linked to the question and justified judgement. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Assess the validity of the claim that social media has made it easier for students to stay informed about global politics.
items.answer: Social media widens access but requires strong media literacy; it is most valuable as a starting point verified by reliable sources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: instant access to diverse voices; first-hand footage; activists and experts share analysis. Markbands (10): 9–10 – focused, balanced argument with specific, accurate examples and a well-supported judgement; 7–8 – relevant examples, counter-claims considered, reasoned judgement; 5–6 – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive, judgement asserted; 3–4 – limited, general knowledge with little evaluation; 1–2 – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Explain how you would structure an answer to a Paper 1 question asking you to evaluate a claim using the sources and your own knowledge.
items.answer: Introduction with clear position; paragraphs weighing evidence for and against from the sources (with explicit references) and own knowledge (specific cases); acknowledgement of source limitations; a reasoned conclusion answering the question.
items.markingKey: Introduction with clear position; paragraphs weighing evidence for and against from the sources (with explicit references) and own knowledge (specific cases); acknowledgement of source limitations; a reasoned conclusion answering the question.

items.stem: Plan an essay in response to: "Evaluate the claim that non-state actors have become more powerful than states." Include a thesis, three main arguments with examples, counter-claims and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis with nuance; arguments e.g. MNC economic/platform power (Meta, Apple), NGO norm-setting (ICBL), violent non-state actors (IS); counter-claims – state regulation (EU DSA), military and legal authority, IS defeat; conclusion – power varies by issue; states remain central.
items.markingKey: Thesis with nuance; arguments e.g. MNC economic/platform power (Meta, Apple), NGO norm-setting (ICBL), violent non-state actors (IS); counter-claims – state regulation (EU DSA), military and legal authority, IS defeat; conclusion – power varies by issue; states remain central.

items.markingKey: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive; disinformation is false information created or spread deliberately to mislead. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between usefulness of a source and reliability of a source.
items.answer: Reliability is how trustworthy or accurate a source is; usefulness depends on the question – even an unreliable, biased source can be very useful for showing a particular perspective.
items.markingKey: Reliability is how trustworthy or accurate a source is; usefulness depends on the question – even an unreliable, biased source can be very useful for showing a particular perspective. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between description and analysis.
items.answer: Description recounts what happened; analysis explains why it happened, its significance and how it relates to the question and concepts.
items.markingKey: Description recounts what happened; analysis explains why it happened, its significance and how it relates to the question and concepts. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is important to use contemporary case studies in Global Politics.
items.answer: The course examines current political issues; contemporary cases show understanding of how concepts apply today and allow candidates to evaluate theories against recent evidence.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The course examines current political issues; contemporary cases show understanding of how concepts apply today and allow candidates to evaluate theories against recent evidence. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Jonas writes: "In a compare and contrast question, writing one paragraph on each source is the best approach." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Separate descriptions rarely compare; a running comparison linking sources point by point on similarities and differences scores more highly.
items.markingKey: Separate descriptions rarely compare; a running comparison linking sources point by point on similarities and differences scores more highly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "A balanced essay should not reach a definite conclusion." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Balance means weighing arguments fairly, but the top markband requires a clear, reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.
items.markingKey: Balance means weighing arguments fairly, but the top markband requires a clear, reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Suggest three types of source you would use to research a new case study and explain the value of each.
items.answer: Primary documents (UN resolutions, treaty texts) – authoritative; quality journalism from different regions – current events and perspectives; academic or think-tank analysis – depth and theory; NGO reports – evidence on rights. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Primary documents (UN resolutions, treaty texts) – authoritative; quality journalism from different regions – current events and perspectives; academic or think-tank analysis – depth and theory; NGO reports – evidence on rights. 1 mark each.

items.stem: Briefly describe political cartoons on climate summits and explain what it reveals about interpreting visual sources.
items.answer: Cartoonists frequently depict leaders making promises while the planet burns or floods. visual sources use symbolism and exaggeration to make a claim, which must be identified and explained like a written argument
items.markingKey: Context (Cartoonists frequently depict leaders making promises while the planet burns or floods.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: visual sources use symbolism and exaggeration to make a claim, which must be identified and explained like a written argument – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interpreting visual sources.

items.stem: With reference to a model essay on soft power, explain how it illustrates the value of comparative analysis in essays.
items.answer: A strong essay contrasts South Korea's Hallyu with China's Confucius Institutes and Russia's RT, and considers measurement (polls such as the Soft Power 30 or Global Soft Power Index). contrasting cases reveal conditions under which soft power works, strengthening evaluation
items.markingKey: Context (A strong essay contrasts South Korea's Hallyu with China's Confucius Institutes and Russia's RT, and considers measurement (polls such as the Soft Power 30 or Global Soft Power Index).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: contrasting cases reveal conditions under which soft power works, strengthening evaluation – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the value of comparative analysis in essays.

items.stem: Using disinformation during the 2016 US election as an example, explain the importance of media literacy.
items.answer: US investigations found that the Russian Internet Research Agency used social media accounts to spread divisive content. state-sponsored disinformation shows why students must evaluate the origin and purpose of online information
items.markingKey: Context (US investigations found that the Russian Internet Research Agency used social media accounts to spread divisive content.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: state-sponsored disinformation shows why students must evaluate the origin and purpose of online information – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of media literacy.

items.stem: A student claims that a biased source is useless for answering a Paper 1 question. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Biased sources can be very useful for revealing an actor's perspective, interests or rhetoric; their limitations must be acknowledged and checked against other evidence.
items.markingKey: Biased sources can be very useful for revealing an actor's perspective, interests or rhetoric; their limitations must be acknowledged and checked against other evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that balance is more important than a clear argument in Paper 2 essays.
items.answer: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: counter-claims required; avoids one-sidedness. Arguments against: top band requires a consistent judgement; balance without conclusion is weak. Supported judgement: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.

items.stem: Explain how you would use one contemporary case study to answer essays on two different syllabus themes.
items.answer: E.g. the Belt and Road Initiative for power (economic statecraft) and development (infrastructure, debt); or Tuvalu for sovereignty and sustainability. Show how the same evidence supports different arguments.
items.markingKey: E.g. the Belt and Road Initiative for power (economic statecraft) and development (infrastructure, debt); or Tuvalu for sovereignty and sustainability. Show how the same evidence supports different arguments.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that own knowledge is more important than the sources in answering Paper 1 evaluation questions?
items.answer: Neither is sufficient alone; the strongest answers integrate sources and own knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: provides context and counter-examples; needed for top markbands. Arguments against: questions are designed around sources; answers must engage with all relevant sources; markbands require both. Supported judgement: Neither is sufficient alone; the strongest answers integrate sources and own knowledge. Markbands: Markbands (scaled to the marks available, five bands): top band – sharply focused, accurate knowledge of concepts, theories and specific examples, well-developed counter-claims and a clear, well-supported judgement; upper-middle – focused, relevant examples, counter-claims addressed, reasoned conclusion; middle – mostly focused, some examples and counter-claims, conclusion stated; lower – limited, mainly descriptive knowledge with little evaluation; bottom – minimal relevant knowledge, no evaluation.

items.stem: "Balance is more important than a clear argument in Paper 2 essays." Using one theoretical perspective and relevant case studies, discuss this view.
items.answer: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: counter-claims required; avoids one-sidedness. Arguments against: top band requires a consistent judgement; balance without conclusion is weak. Supported judgement: Balance is necessary but must serve a clear argument that reaches a supported conclusion. Markbands (15): 13–15 – sharply focused on the demands of the question; detailed, accurate knowledge of relevant concepts, theories and specific contemporary examples; well-developed, balanced counter-claims; a clear, consistent and well-supported conclusion. 10–12 – focused and well structured; relevant, accurate knowledge and examples; counter-claims addressed; reasoned conclusion. 7–9 – mostly focused; relevant knowledge with some examples; some counter-claims; conclusion stated. 4–6 – some understanding of the demands; limited or general knowledge, mainly descriptive; little evaluation. 1–3 – little understanding; minimal relevant knowledge; no evaluation. 0 – does not reach the standard of band 1.
